reconcile.connective: Adam Clarke concedes the disciples' ignorance is a genuine reproach, but reads it as an undesigned mark of the Gospel's honesty rather than a fabrication.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman argues the detailed passion predictions are later, Markan vaticinia ex eventu — so the disciples' ignorance in John 20:9 reflects an earlier tradition.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet of the New Millennium
skeptic.attribution: Bart D. Ehrman, Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet of the New Millennium (Oxford University Press, 1999), pp. 217-220

excerpts.excerpt_text: It was certainly a reproach to the disciples that they had not understood this prophecy, when our Lord had given them often the most direct information concerning it. … However, this ingenuous confession of John, in a matter so dishonorable to himself, is a full proof of his sincerity, and of the truth of his narration.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Clarke concedes the disciples' failure to grasp the resurrection despite Jesus' repeated direct forewarning was a genuine 'reproach,' then reframes that admitted tension as evidence of John's honesty — directly engaging the predictions-vs-John-20:9 gap rather than glossing over it.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke's note on John 20:9 directly concedes and answers this tension (the disciples' ignorance is a 'reproach' given Jesus' repeated direct forewarning), reading it as an undesigned mark of Gospel honesty rather than a fabrication.
